entry.title: Five rules for AI over official statistics
entry.summary: The five conditions UBOS wrote down before releasing Sanyu, its AI assistant over official statistics, and why each one exists.
entry.content:
Generative systems are arriving in statistical dissemination across the continent this year, often procured quickly and judged more on how fluent they sound than on whether the numbers are right. A model that produces a confident, wrong district population hands the reputational bill to the office that published it. Official statistics carry value only because the public accepts the figure.

So before Sanyu goes out as a public service of the Bureau, we wrote down the conditions we had to meet to feel safe releasing it. Five clauses, each one drawn from something the build itself forced on us. They're short enough to check.

1. Figures originate in the statistical system

The model selects what to retrieve; the database supplies the value. A number reaches the user only when a structured query returned it. This is the whole architecture in one sentence. The language model never generates a figure, it emits a typed function call, and the verified result is placed into the answer verbatim.

2. Every figure carries its source

Source table, survey or census, reference period and geography travel with the value, in a form the user can follow back to the publication. Charts render from the same verified values as the surrounding text, so a picture can't disagree with its caption.

3. The system declines outside its data

Where a question falls beyond published statistics, the correct response says so plainly. Silence about a limit counts as a defect. This one was harder to build than it sounds, because a fluent model would much rather answer.

4. Evaluation is published before launch

A named benchmark with ground truth, plus a regression suite that asserts exact published figures, runs automatically on every build. Ours has 45 deterministic tests, including a set of golden facts that must match the printed census tables to the digit. The results are public.

5. A statistician signs

Generated narrative passes a named human reviewer before publication. The machine drafts; the office remains the author.

The code demonstrates that the conditions are achievable, because the system standing beside it meets them.

None of these rules is about a particular vendor or model. They're conditions any statistics office could adopt this year, and we'd like other offices to argue with them, adapt them, and tell us what we missed. The technical details of how Sanyu meets them are on the work page.

entry.title: A week in Rome with SDMX
entry.summary: Notes from the 10th SDMX Global Conference in Rome, where UBOS presented its AI-enabled statistics pipeline, and what changed back home.
entry.content:
Ivan Atwiine and I spent last week at the 10th SDMX Global Conference in Rome, hosted by the Bank of Italy. Three days of plenaries, then two days of training. The theme was "Smarter data for better insights", and the invitation had asked for exactly the kind of work we do: AI and machine learning applied to statistical pipelines, and dissemination tools that people actually use.

We went to talk about the pipeline. The paper, "From fragmentation to intelligence", describes how UBOS pulls administrative, survey and census data straight from source systems into one platform, validates it on the way in, and publishes it through the national dashboard. The rule-based checks catch the obvious; the machine learning helps with anomalies, cleaning and classifying community-level submissions. It's the plumbing behind everything else the Bureau now does with data.

What I took home

SDMX is a join key, not a file format. I had been treating it as a way to publish. The better way to see it: once two datasets share the same concepts, code lists and dimensions, a question that crosses them becomes cheap to answer. That is precisely what a chatbot over official statistics needs. Most of the effort in grounding a language model is agreeing on what an indicator means, and SDMX is that agreement, written down.

Validation can be data too. The sessions on SDMX 3.0 and VTL, the validation and transformation language, described rules as something you exchange rather than something buried in a script. We write ours in Python. Some of them should probably live next to the data instead.

Everyone's problem is fragmentation. Central banks, statistical offices, international agencies: the stories differed in scale, not in kind. The exciting demos all rested on the boring, careful part, which is people agreeing on structure. That was reassuring. It is the part we can control.

The two training days made the tooling concrete: data structure definitions, dataflows, registries. It's one thing to read the standard, another to build a dataflow with someone who has done it a hundred times and watch where they slow down.

What changed back home

We came back and started a prototype: take survey tables from the demographic and health survey and the household survey, and turn them into SDMX-ready structures. Reusable structure definitions by table shape rather than one per table, and a crosswalk of indicators so we can say quickly whether a figure exists in one survey, the other, or both. It's the first step toward cross-dataset retrieval, chatbot queries that span surveys, and briefs that write themselves from verified numbers.

Rome itself: warm, loud, and exactly as good at coffee as advertised.
